title: Two Music Giants Sue an AI Lab Over Tens of Thousands of Songs
hook: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic over copyrighted works — and the damages math shows why these training-data cases are existential, not incidental.
key_points: The Verge reported on August 29, 2026 that Sony Music and Warner Chappell sued Anthropic.
Filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.
The claim covers 'tens of thousands' of copyrighted works.
They seek up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each stripping of copyright data.
Stripping identifying copyright information is a separate legal claim from the copying itself.
Multiply per-work damages by tens of thousands and the exposure dwarfs most licensing deals.
content_html: On August 29, 2026, The Verge reported that Sony Music and Warner Chappell filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, seeking damages over "tens of thousands" of copyrighted works. They're asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance where identifying copyright data was stripped.
extra_html:
The arithmetic is the story. A single $150,000 claim is a rounding error for a large company; the same figure multiplied across tens of thousands of works is the kind of number that decides whether a business exists. That's why the training-data question — does building a model on copyrighted material require a licence? — keeps landing in court rather than being settled by a handshake.

Note also the second claim. Removing the copyright information attached to a work is treated as a distinct violation from copying it, with its own per-instance damages. It's a technical point that matters in practice, because bulk-scraped training data routinely arrives stripped of whoever made it. None of this is decided yet: a filed complaint is an allegation, and courts have been reaching different conclusions about where the line falls.

related.title: A Judge Approves Anthropic's $1.5B Payout to Authors
related.hook: A court signed off on Anthropic paying authors $1.5 billion — about $3,000 a book — for training its AI on their work. The rare case where the copyright fight ended in a check.

related.title: Who Owns AI's Output?
related.hook: You typed the prompt, the AI made the image — so who owns it? The law is genuinely unsettled, and the answer depends on where you are and how much was really you.

related.title: A Hack Exposed What an AI Music Generator Trained On
related.hook: Suno never said what music trained its AI. A hacking incident did the talking instead, reportedly exposing millions of songs and lyrics scraped from YouTube, Genius, and Deezer.

flashcards.prompt: Why are per-work damages the key number in AI copyright suits?

choices.text: Statutory damages are multiplied by every work involved — here, tens of thousands
Courts cap total damages at the per-work figure
Per-work damages replace any finding of infringement
The figure sets the price of a future licence

flashcards.explanation_html: Up to $150,000 per work sounds survivable until it's multiplied by tens of thousands of works — that's what makes these cases existential.

flashcards.prompt: What's the separate claim about 'stripping copyright data'?
flashcards.back_html: Removing the identifying copyright information attached to a work is its own violation — the suit seeks up to $25,000 for each instance.

flashcards.prompt: What question do music-industry suits like this one actually test?
flashcards.back_html: Whether training an AI model on copyrighted recordings requires a licence, or counts as permitted use. Courts are still working it out.
